what_it_does: Diffractive neural networks are a class of physical AI systems where computation happens by shaping how a wave (light or sound) diffracts — bends and scatters — through a series of precisely patterned layers, much like how a prism splits light. Until now, these systems have been built mostly for light (optical). This paper adapts the idea to acoustic waves, specifically surface acoustic waves (SAW) — vibrations that travel along the surface of a solid material, commonly used in microelectronics filters and sensors. The goal is an analog AI sensor that can diagnose multiple biological markers directly in hardware without needing a digital processor. Training the diffractive pattern is the core challenge: physics simulations (finite element analysis, which numerically solves wave equations on a mesh) are accurate but slow, while gradient descent (the standard AI training algorithm) is fast but ignores hardware physics. The paper combines both by alternating between physics simulations and gradient-based updates to co-optimize the diffractive pattern for the real SAW device.
